titre: The King Must Now Say Why He Imprisons
accroche: In 1627, dozens of Englishmen are imprisoned without being given any reason, until five of them take the case before the judges.
contenu_vulgarise:
## Paying Without Parliament

In 1626 and 1627, Charles I needs money to finance the war against Spain, under way since 1625 and already marked by the failure of the Cadiz expedition, but Parliament, which he has just dissolved, has voted him no subsidy. He then imposes a “forced loan”: every well-off subject must advance the Crown a sum fixed in advance. Refusing means prison. At least seventy-six men choose imprisonment over payment.

## A Reason That Does Not Exist

Among them, five knights (Thomas Darnell, John Corbet, Walter Erle, John Heveningham, and Edmund Hampden) ask the Court of King's Bench to grant habeas corpus: they want to be told, as procedure requires, the specific reason for which they are held. The Crown's answer comes down to five words of legal Latin: *per speciale mandatum domini regis*, by special command of the king himself. No charge to examine. In November 1627, Chief Justice Nicholas Hyde refuses to release them on bail: in the absence of a stated reason, he says, it must be presumed that this is a matter of state that the court need not hear.

The decision, known as Darnell's Case, shocks well beyond the five plaintiffs: it amounts to saying that no law requires the Crown to justify an arrest. The need for money forces Charles I to recall Parliament in 1628, where the majority of the newly elected members prove hostile to the Crown.

## A Text, Not a New Trial

Rather than a new judgment, Parliament chooses another instrument: a solemn petition, drafted by a committee chaired by Edward Coke, who is back as a mere member of Parliament eighteen years after judging the Bonham case. The text demands four guarantees: no tax or forced loan without Parliament's consent, no imprisonment without a stated reason, no forced quartering of soldiers in private homes, and no martial law in peacetime.

On June 2, 1628, Charles I first attempts a half-hearted acceptance; both houses demand an unambiguous answer. On June 7, he yields and pronounces the formula reserved for petitions of right: “Soit droit fait come est desire” (“Let right be done as is desired”). The Petition of Right becomes law of the realm, though it never stops Charles I, in the years that follow, from continuing to levy taxes without Parliament.

carte.punch: At least seventy-six Englishmen choose prison over a forced loan decided without Parliament.
carte.idee: In 1627, dozens of Englishmen refuse a forced loan decided without Parliament and are imprisoned with no stated reason. Five of them go to court; their failure leads Parliament to force the Petition of Right on the king in 1628: no more arrests without a stated cause.

quiz.question: Why does the Court of King's Bench refuse, in 1627, to release the five imprisoned knights on bail?
choix: Because they had publicly admitted organizing a rebellion against the king
Because no ground for the charge was stated, which the court interprets as a matter of state secrecy
Because the Petition of Right did not yet exist to protect them in 1627
Because Parliament itself had called for their detention to be maintained
quiz.explication: The Crown invokes a “special command of the king” without detailing any specific charge; the court holds that, in the absence of a stated reason, the matter must fall under state secrecy and refuses to examine its legality: exactly what the Petition of Right will forbid the following year.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why does Charles I impose a “forced loan” in 1626-1627?
choix: To make up for a bad harvest that deprives the state of tax revenue
To finance the war against Spain, without the consent of a Parliament he has dissolved
To repay the Crown's personal debts to Scotland
To pay for building a new war fleet against the United Provinces
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Charles I needs money for the war against Spain, but the Parliament he has just dissolved voted him no subsidy, hence the forced loan imposed on well-off subjects.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Who chairs the committee that drafts the text of the Petition of Right in 1628?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: It is Edward Coke, back as a mere member of Parliament eighteen years after judging the Bonham case, who chairs the committee charged with drafting the Petition of Right.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What other guarantees does the Petition of Right demand, besides the ban on imprisonment without a stated reason?
choix: The permanent abolition of the Court of King's Bench
The transformation of Parliament into the kingdom's supreme court
No tax and no forced quartering of soldiers without Parliament's consent
The creation of a permanent veto for the House of Lords
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The text also demands that no tax or forced loan be levied without Parliament, and that no soldier be quartered by force in private homes, two grievances born of the forced loan of 1626-1627.
